texts.facts: As the controversy involved in these criminal misc. petitions is common, therefore, they are being decided by this common order. The defects pointed out by the Registry are minor in nature, (6 of 13) [CRLMP-2472/2015] therefore, the same are waived. These criminal misc. petitions have been filed by the petitioner being aggrieved with the order dated 11.08.2015 passed by the Additional Sessions Judge No.2, Barmer (hereinafter referred to as 'the revisional court') in Criminal Revision Petition Nos.42/2015(53/13), 34/2015(56/13), Anil Mehta vs State & Anr on 20 February, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/9533563/ 4 40/2015(14/13), 38/2015(54/13), 39/2015(55/13), 31/2015(49/13), 37/2015(13/13), 30/2015(16/13), 36/2015(17/13), 32/2015(50/13), 45/2015(15/13), 33/2015(57/13), 43/2015(48/13) and 44/2015(47/13) respectively, whereby the revisional court has dismissed the aforesaid revision petitions. The aforesaid criminal revision petitions were preferred by the petitioner against the orders dated 11.02.2012 passed by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Barmer (hereinafter referred to as 'the trial court') in Criminal Complaint Nos.119/2008, 123/2008, 134/2008, 129/2008, 122/2008, 128/2008, 132/2008, 131/2008, 130/2008, 126/2008, 133/2008, 121/2008, 124/2008 and 120/2008 respectively, whereby it has dismissed the applications preferred by the petitioner under Section 468 Cr.P.C. with a prayer for quashing the orders dated 10.03.2008 of taking cognizance against the petitioner in various criminal complaints for the offence punishable under Sections 7/16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act of 1954'). Brief facts of the case are that on 22.12.2004 and 23.12.2004, the Food Inspector posted in the Office of Chief Medical and Health Officer, Barmer conducted a sudden check in (7 of 13) [CRLMP-2472/2015] the shop belonging to the petitioner, as per the order of Chief Medical and Health Officer, Barmer. The petitioner is in business of trading of ghee and the Food Inspector collected several samples of ghee from the shop of the petitioner. The said samples of ghee were properly sealed and sent to the Chemical Analyst for chemical examination and as per the report, the same were found adulterated then the complaints were filed before the trial court, on which the trial court vide orders dated 10.03.2008 took cognizance against the petitioner for the offence punishable under Section 7/16 of the Act of 1954. Thereafter the matters were proceeded further before the trial court, however, in the year 2012 the petitioner moved applications before the trial court in those complaints and prayed that the orders of taking cognizance be [LEAKAGE_MASK] as the cognizance has been taken beyond the period of limitation. The case of the petitioner is to the effect that the samples of ghee were collected from his shop on 22.12.2004 and 23.12.2004, whereas the cognizance was taken by the trial court on 10.03.2008. It is contended that for the offence punishable under Section 7/16 of the Act of 1954, the limitation for taking cognizance is three years, however, in the complaints, filed against the petitioner, the cognizance was taken against him after expiry of three years, therefore, the orders of taking cognizance be [LEAKAGE_MASK]. The trial court, after hearing the counsel for the petitioner, vide order dated 11.02.2012 has rejected those applications while observing that it has no jurisdiction to review its orders of taking (8 of 13) [CRLMP-2472/2015] cognizance in those complaints and further observed that if there is any technical illegality in the orders of taking cognizance against the petitioner, the petitioner can take benefit of the same at the time of the decision of the cases filed against him. Being aggrieved with the order dated 11.02.2012, the petitioner preferred aforementioned criminal revision petitions before the revisional court, which came to be dismissed by the revisional court vide order dated 11.08.2015. The revisional court has observed that it appears from the record that the Food Inspector, who had collected the samples of ghee from the shop of the petitioner, was suspended and thereafter another Food Inspector was appointed to file complaints against the Anil Mehta vs State & Anr on 20 February, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/9533563/ 5 petitioner and looking to this fact and as per Section 473 Cr.P.C., if sufficient cause is available, the Court can take cognizance for an offence after expiry of the period of limitation. After observing this, the revisional court has dismissed the revision petitions filed by the petitioner.
texts.arguments: Being aggrieved with this the petitioner has preferred these criminal misc. petitions under Section 482 Cr.P.C. Learned counsel for the petitioner has submitted that it is settled proposition of law that cognizance of an offence beyond the period of limitation is bad in the eye of law and an accused person cannot be prosecuted beyond the period of limitation. It is also contended that as per Section 473 Cr.P.C., for condoning the delay, the Court, which is taking cognizance, has to satisfy that the delay has been properly explained and has to record its satisfaction to the effect that delay has been properly explained (9 of 13) [CRLMP-2472/2015] and it is necessary to condon the delay in the interest of justice, however, in the present cases, the trial court while taking cognizance has neither condoned the delay nor specified the reasons for condoning the delay and, therefore, the said orders are bad in the eye of law. It is contended that the revisional court without taking into consideration this aspect of the matters has illegally rejected the revision petitions filed by the petitioner. In support of the above contention learned counsel for the petitioner has placed reliance on the decision of Hon'ble Supreme Court rendered in Srinivas Pal Vs. Union Territory of Arunachal Pradesh reported in AIR 1988 SC 1729, the decision of Karnataka High Court rendered in State of Karnataka Vs. Vedavati reported in 1978 Cri.L.J. 1375, the decision of this Court rendered in Panney Singh & Ors. Vs. State of Rajasthan reported in 1980 Cri.L.J. 339, the decision of Bombay High Court rendered in Sharadchandra Vinayak Dongre & Ors. Vs. State of Maharashtra reported in 1991 Cri.L.J. 3329, the decision of Calcutta High Court rendered in Yukub Ali Saranj & Ors. Vs. The State of W.B. reported in 1995 Cri.L.J. 4077 and the decision of Gauhati High Court at Kohima Bench rendered in K. Vikheho Sema Vs. State of Nagaland reported in 2007 Cri.L.J. 4266. Per contra, learned Public Prosecutor has opposed the prayer of the petitioner and submitted that the revisional court has not committed any illegality in passing the impugned order and, therefore, no interference is called for. Heard the learned counsel for the parties and perused the (10 of 13) [CRLMP-2472/2015] impugned order. It is not in dispute that the Food Inspector collected the samples of ghee from the shop of the petitioner on 22.12.2004 and 23.12.2004. The said samples of ghee were found to be adulterated as per the report of the Chemical Analyst. It is also not in dispute that the complaints against the petitioner were filed on 10.03.2008 i.e. after expiry of three years from the date of collection of samples of ghee. Learned counsel for the petitioner has not disputed the fact that the Food Inspector, who had collected the samples of ghee from the shop of the petitioner, was suspended and another Food Inspector was appointed for filing complaints against the petitioner. Anil Mehta vs State & Anr on 20 February, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/9533563/ 6 The trial court has observed that it cannot alter or cancel the orders of taking cognizance passed by it earlier and this Court is of the opinion that the trial court has rightly observed so in view of the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court rendered in Adalat Prasad Vs. Roopal Jindal & Ors. reported in (2004) 7 SCC 338, wherein it has been held as under:- "But after taking cognizance of the complaint and examining the complainant and the witnesses if he is satisfied that there is sufficient ground to proceed with the complaint he (11 of 13) [CRLMP-2472/2015] can issue process by way of summons under section 204 of the Code. It is true that if a Magistrate takes cognizance of an offence, issues process without there being any allegation against the accused or any material implicating the accused or in contravention of provision of Sections 200 & 202, the order of the Magistrate may be vitiated, but then the relief an aggrieved accused can obtain at that stage is not by invoking Section 203 of the Code because the Criminal Procedure Code does not contemplate a review of an order. ..." Moreover, there is another aspect in those cases that in (12 of 13) [CRLMP-2472/2015] those complaints filed against the petitioner, the Food Inspector has mentioned that the complaints against the petitioner are filed after obtaining prosecution sanction from the Chief Medical and Health Officer concerned. Anil Mehta vs State & Anr on 20 February, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/9533563/ 7 Sub-section (3) of Section 470 Cr.P.C. provides that if before institution of any prosecution of an offence against a person, previous consent or sanction of the government or any authority is required then time required for obtaining such consent or sanction shall be excluded. Sub-section (3) of Section 470 Cr.P.C. reads as under :- "(3) Where notice of prosecution for an offence has been given, or where , under any law for the time being in force, the previous consent or sanction of the Government or any other authority is required for the institution of any prosecution for an offence, than, in computing the period of limitation, the period of such notice or, as the case may be, the time required for obtaining such consent or sanction shall be excluded. Explanation.--In computing the time required for obtaining the consent or sanction of the Government or any other authority , the date on which the application was made for obtaining the consent or sanction and the date of receipt of the order of the Government or other authority shall both be excluded."
